title: David's great wrong (2 Samuel 11)
hook: a king on a rooftop takes Bathsheba and arranges her husband's death

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mephibosheth, given a seat at the king's table. Your line was always at my table.

The chapter opens "at the time when kings go forth to battle," and adds a quiet line: "But David tarried still at Jerusalem." One evening he gets up from his bed and walks on the palace roof, and from up there he sees a woman bathing. He asks who she is. The answer comes back with her name and, pointedly, her husband's: Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his soldiers, away at the war. The king knows exactly who she is. And he sends for her anyway.

The verbs belong to the king: "David sent messengers, and took her." Sent, took. Some readers point out that Bathsheba had little room to say no, and the text gives her no words at all until a message she sends back: "I am with child." Then the cover-up. David calls Uriah home from the war, and sends him off to his house, hoping the child will seem to be his. Uriah sleeps at the palace door with the servants instead. Asked why, the soldier answers with a loyalty that shames the king: "The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents; and my lord Joab, and the servants of my lord, are encamped in the open fields; shall I then go into mine house, to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife?" David gets him drunk the next night; he still doesn't go home. So David writes to his general, and has Uriah carry the letter himself: "Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die." Other soldiers die with him. David sends back a smooth message: don't let this trouble you; the sword devours one as well as another. Then he marries Bathsheba. For a moment it looks like he got away with it. The chapter's last line says otherwise: "But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD." This is the same man who spared Saul in the cave. The text doesn't explain the change. Some readers point to how much power he now had, and how few people could tell him no.

Hold in mind Bathsheba, who speaks only once in this chapter, and Uriah, carrying his own death warrant without knowing it. Then let your mind move to people today who have been used or silenced by someone with power over them, at work, at home, in a church; you don't need names. If you pray, pray for them in your own words or in silence; if not, simply hold them in mind with care.
Uriah. The loyal soldier whose wife David took, and whom David then arranged to have killed in battle.
Your line: power can rot. Sent, took: two short verbs, and a long fall. Day seven hundred twenty-three, done.

howItsDone: Some Christians read 2 Samuel 11 as a sobering story about the abuse of power and the way one wrong leads to the next, and read it alongside Nathan's rebuke and Psalm 51.

fork.setup: you're Uriah. the king has called you home from the war and told you to go down to your house. what do you do?
options: go home and rest with your wife.
sleep at the palace door with the servants.

fork.reveal: he sleeps at the door of the king's house. how can he go home, he says, while the ark and the army are in tents? his loyalty undoes the cover-up.

what it means: a king uses his power to take a married woman, then has her husband killed to hide it.
what a scholar hears: the king's verbs, sent and took; Bathsheba's only words, I am with child; and Uriah, an outsider, more loyal than the king.

chat.says: In the David and Bathsheba story, why does Uriah matter so much?
options: He stayed loyal, and David still had him killed to cover his own sin.
He was a traitor, so David was right to put him in the front line.
He found out about David and tried to take the throne for himself.
chat.meaning: Uriah wouldn't go home while the army camped in the field; David sent him to the front to die, and it displeased the LORD.

Bathsheba.meaning: Uriah's wife, whom King David sent for and took

notes: Sensitive: the script follows the text ('sent... and took her') and frames this as abuse of royal power. 'Some readers point out that Bathsheba had little room to say no'; readings of Bathsheba's agency differ. Confirm tone.
David's message to Joab paraphrased from 11:25; Uriah drunk from 11:13; other soldiers die from 11:17.
Index hook calls it 'a king on a rooftop'; the text says David walked on the roof of the king's house and saw her from there (11:2).
The practice keeps prayer optional and offers no written words.

Editor: the narrator's verdict on David's heart ('nothing in his heart changed... what changed was how much power he had') is now attributed to 'some readers', since the text gives no reason; hook no longer opens on a quotation (yesterday's did); howItsDone 'often discussed' softened.
Audit: Bathsheba's 'I am with child' is a message she sends (11:5), not words spoken to David; the teach now says so.
